newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Digital democracy inflamed.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Digital democracy inflamed.

text.p: With an estimated 6 billion e-mail messages floating around the planet each year it is hardly surprising that the original message can get misconstrued, get lost or, heaven forbid, get a little nasty.
Sometimes called the fax machine of the 1990s, e-mail has obviously become the indispensable tool of the digital world.
This new tool has not wiped out snail mail (mail delivered by the human hand) just yet, but it has wrought some major changes, including access to people on a most instant and intimate level.

It is estimated that with just a few keystrokes you can have access to some 60 million people around the world -- and that includes everyone from the world's most powerful, your boss, as well as your loved ones and even prospective loved ones.
But with any new toy that men and women create there are always a few drawbacks we have to get used to.
E-mail etiquette is whole new field and it is a bit of a growth industry on the Net judging by all the World Wide Web pages set up to advise us.

Thanks to the good advice, many of us have learned to look down upon people who "spam" us with unwanted advertising in our inboxes and we are also aware that a message all in caps can appear rather aggressive to the reader.
Albion, a San Francisco-based Internet publisher, publishes some sound rules on how to be a responsible e-mailer (www.albion.com/netiquette/corerules.html):
- Rule 1: Remember the Human.
- Rule 2: Adhere to the same standards of behavior online that you follow in real life.
- Rule 3: Know where you are in cyberspace.
- Rule 4: Respect other people's time and bandwidth.
- Rule 5: Make yourself look good online.
- Rule 6: Share expert knowledge.
- Rule 7: Help keep flame wars under control.
- Rule 8: Respect other people's privacy.
- Rule 9: Don't abuse your power.
- Rule 10: Be forgiving of other people's mistakes.

Any writer brave enough to publish on the Net (complete with e-mail address) will tell you what a searing experience it can be to read the responses one gets by daring to offer an opinion on any given subject.

Experienced surfers will tell you that it is easy to overreact to e-mail that at first glance can appear rather harsh. Some believe the experience of reading e-mail a few inches from the screen can be a lot different when the message is printed out.

But there is no getting away from a genuine flame from some angry surfer out there. Flame hate mail typically employs strong language, personal attacks and an intermingling of capitalized words with the lower case variety that make the message somewhat akin to a digital ransom note.

Some of this can be attributed to a Wizard of Oz syndrome. That is some people feel empowered and somewhat heartless when sitting behind a big machine. The machine allows them to speak in a powerful voice -- albeit digital -- as they dash off a tough note to someone who was foolhardy enough to leave an e-mail address on the Net.

But flaming is also an essential part of the Net because for the first time people are really empowered to voice their opinions. If someone spouted off in a newspaper, in a magazine or on TV, there didn't use to be an effective way to reply to those opinions -- other than a letter to the editor a few weeks or months later.
Now the playing field is leveled and a true lively, vocal democracy is thriving on the Net and there is little hope of anyone corraling this new found freedom of e-mail anytime soon.
